title: A "Stunning" Love Letter to Viral Texts
intro: Like most nineteenth-century newspapers, [_The Raftsman's Journal_](https://www.loc.gov/item/sn85054616/) sought to connect its readers in rural Clearfield, Pennsylvania with wider worlds of news, information, and literature. Whether published in major metropolitan areas such as New York, Boston, and Philadelphia; in smaller cities such as Wheeling or Nashville; or in rural towns such as Clearfield, nineteenth-century newspapers relied on networks of exchange for much of their content. Newspaper editors subscribed to each others' newspapers, which came to them in the mail on post roads or, later, railroads.

waypoints.title: Newspaper Exchanges
waypoints.body:
When exchange papers arrived, editors would comb through them to find content their readers would appreciate, which they would then clip out with scissors and paste on sheets for their compositors to set in new type for the next daily, weekly, or irregular edition, sometimes changing the original text in the process. Sometimes a clipping would not be needed immediately, but would be saved for later use. In the [Viral Texts Project](https://viraltexts.org), we study this "exchange system," and often find clusters of reprinted texts that circulated in this way around the country over years or even decades. When texts were circulating, editors would observe that they were ["going the rounds."](#801896d3-9f60-4468-bdf8-2efff26fa971)

Thus texts of all kinds—news, of course, but also [fiction](#97e28e6d-e0d3-43c8-bfff-7a60f37a3f50), [poetry](#b246052a-1619-4621-bb4e-37541feec83c), [vignettes](#801896d3-9f60-4468-bdf8-2efff26fa971), how-to columns, [lists](#ef824ae1-c026-407c-8ffe-2e0f838431d2), [descriptions of scientific and historical curiosities](#ceafac2d-6aeb-48fb-8d0b-21a3c8127d59), [etiquette](#066356d8-ff9d-4856-ac7b-6befd700dcf6), [medical and health notes](#a4075ee4-40f9-49ac-b958-0d58017f408e), [business advice](#91c754a2-0b3b-4c0f-8094-310f4bf708ef), [parenting advice](#8d3e1d3f-ff05-421b-bf8d-c55517daf2c8), recipes, [religious affirmations](#55e9f780-e880-4ac1-9061-03da8eef27e5), [jokes](#10c9fe1b-92c6-4c9f-bd4a-452a1d894178), and more—circulated around the country, connecting readers from New England to New Orleans to California through shared texts.

This exhibit is intended to hint at the breadth—and the oddities—of nineteenth-century reprinting that we have found thus far in the Viral Texts Project. If you peruse the page, you will find other articles that link to reprints in our database. Click on them to browse versions that appeared in other newspapers and see how reprinting worked in practice.

———— § § § ————

waypoints.title: A "stunning" Love Letter
waypoints.body:
We focus, however, on the "sublimely 'splendiferous'" love letter in the middle of the page, which was itself [reprinted in more than 100 newspapers](https://clusters.viraltexts.org/cluster/4408319?search_term=sublimely+splendiferous), where its details—including the addressee's name—shifted. 

This is one of our favorite "viral texts": it's funny and over the top—no doubt both reasons for its popularity—but in its humor it speaks also to many common themes across the widely-reprinted texts we have found. To that end, we have carefully annotated this edition of "A 'stunning' Love Letter" to point out to related texts in our database. We are not claiming that the writer of "Love Letter" had these other texts in mind. Instead, we hope this provides a fun way to begin exploring the vast range of topics, genres, styles, and tones that comprised the nineteenth-century newspaper.

> A "stunning" Love Letter.
> 
> The following is [sublimely 'splendiferous,'](#wl-splendiferous) and we cecommend it as a model to letter writers:
> 
> [MY DEAR MISS C.](#wl-miss-c)—Every time I think of you [my heart flops up and down like a churn dasher](#wl-churn-dasher). Sensations of unutterable joy creep over it like [young goats over a stable roof](#wl-young-goats), and thrill through it like [Spanish needles through a pair of tow linen trowsers](#wl-spanish-needles). As [a gosling swimeth with delight in a mud-puddle, so swim I in a sea of glory](#wl-gosling). Visions of ecstatic rapture, [thicker than the hairs in a blacking brush](#wl-blacking-brush), and [brighter than the hue of the humming bird's pinions](#wl-humming-bird), visi me in my slumbers, and borne on their visible wings, your image stands before me, and [I reach out to grasp it, like a pointer snapping at a blue bottle fly](#wl-blue-bottle-fly). When I first beheld your angelic perfections, I was bewildered, and [my brain whirled about like a bumble bee under a glass tumbler](#wl-bumble-bee). [My eyes stood open like cellar doors in a country town](#wl-cellar-doors), and I lifted up my ears to catch the silvery accents of your voice. [My tongue refused to wag](#wl-tongue-wag), and [in silent adoration I drank in the sweet infection of love as a thirsty man swalloweth a hot whiskey punch](#wl-whiskey-punch). Since the light of your face fell upon my life, I sometimes feel as if I could [lift myself up by my bootstraps to the top of the presbyterian steeple, and pull the bell rope for singing school](#wl-presbyterian-steeple). Day and night you are in my thoughts. When [Aurora, blushing like a bride, rises from her saffron couch](#wl-aurora); and when [the jay bird pipes his tuneful lay in the apple tree](#wl-jay-bird), by the spring house; when [the chanticleer's shrill clarion heralds the coming morn](#wl-chanticleer); when [the awakened pig ariseth from his bed and grunteth](#wl-pig-ariseth), and goeth for his morning refreshments; when [the drowsy beetle wheels his drowning flight, at sultry noontide](#wl-beetle-drowning), and when [the lowing cows come home at milking time](#wl-milking-time), I think of thee; and like a piece of gum elastic, [my heart seems to stretch clean across my bosom](#wl-gum-elastic). Your [hair is like the mane of a sorrel horse, powdered with gold](#wl-sorrel-horse); and [the brass pin skewered through your waterfall, fills me with unbounded awe](#wl-unbounded-awe). [Your forehead is smoothar than the elbow of an old coat](#wl-your-forehead). Your eyes are glorious to behold. [In their liquid depths I see legions of little Cupids](#wl-little-cupids), [bathing like a cohort of ants in an old army cracker](#wl-army-cracker). When their fire hit upon my manly breast, [it penetrated my entire anatomy like a load of bird-shot would go thro a rotten apple](#wl-rotten-apple). [Your nose is from a chunk of Parian marble, and your mouth puckered with sweetness](#wl-parian-marble). [Nectar lingers on your lips like honey on a bear's paw](#wl-bears-paw), and [myriads of unfledged kisses are there ready to fly out an light somewhere, like blue birds out of the parent's nest](#wl-blue-birds). [Your laugh rings on my ears like the wind-harp's strains, or the bleat of a stray lamb on the bleak hillside](#wl-wind-harp). [The dimples in your cheek are like bowers in beds of roses](#wl-bowers-roses), or [hollows in a cake of home-made sugar](#wl-home-made-sugar).
> 
> I am dying to fly to your presence and [pour out the burning eloquence of my love](#wl-eloquence-coffee), [as a thrifty house wife pours out coffee](#wl-thrifty-housewife). Away from you I am as [melancholy as a sick rat](#wl-sick-rat). Sometimes I can hear [the June bugs of despondency buzzing in my ears](#wl-june-bugs), and feel [the cold lizards of despair crawling down my back](#wl-cold-lizards). [Uncouth feats, like a thousand minnows, nibble at my spirits](#wl-thousand-minnows), and [my soul is pierced through with doubts, as an old cheese with skippers](#wl-cheese-skippers).
> 
> My love for you is [stronger than the smell of Coffy's patent butter, or the kick of a young cow](#wl-coffys-butter), and [more unselfish than a kitten's first caterwaul](#wl-caterwaul). As the song bird hankers for the light of day, [the cautious mouse for the fresh bacon in the trap, as a lean pup hankers after new milk](#wl-lean-pup), so I long for thee.
> 
> You are [fairer than a speckled pullet](#wl-speckled-pullet), [sweeter than a yankee doughnut fried in sorgum molasses](#wl-sorgum-molasses), [brighter than the topknot plumage in the head of a muscovy duck](#wl-muscovy-duck). [You are candy kisses, raisins, and pound cake and sweetened toddy altogether](#wl-candy-kisses).
> 
> If these few remarks will enable you to see the inside of my soul, and me to win your affections, I shall be as [happy as a woodpecker on a cherry tree, or a stage horse in a green pasture](#wl-woodpecker). If you cannot reciprocate my thrilling passion, I will [pine away like a poisoned bedbug](#wl-poisoned-bedbug), and [falling away from the flourishing vine of life, and untimely branch](#wl-untimely-branch); and in the coming years, when the shadows grow from the hills, and [the philisophic frog sings his cheerful evening hymns](#wl-frog-hymns), you, happy in another's love, [can come and drop a tear and catch a cold upon the last resting place of](#wl-catch-a-cold),
> 
> [JULIUS EPAMINONDAS MUGGINS](#wl-signature).

waypoints.title: Splendiferous
waypoints.body: The word "splendiferous" tells us we're not to take this piece seriously. Like other "splendiferous" reprinted pieces, this "Love Letter" has its tongue planted firmly in its cheek.

waypoints.title: Miss C.
waypoints.body: The name of the beloved changed frequently as this love letter circulated through US newspapers. Like most "viral texts," this piece was fungible, and could be changed to suit the needs (or whims) of particular editors and particular readers — which is why "Miss C." appears under other names in other printings.

waypoints.title: Humming Bird
waypoints.body: The hummingbird's beauty features not only in our love letter but also in a sometimes-reprinted fable about judging by appearances — morality fables being a popular genre for reprinting, easily adapted to any political, personal, or social situation.

waypoints.title: Chanticleer's Shrill Clarion
waypoints.body:
Given its literary origins, it's perhaps unsurprising that "chanticleer" appears mostly in poems, such as James Russell Lowell's "The Snow-Fall," reprinted in more than 50 newspapers, including The Cheyenne Transporter, published by the Cheyenne-Arapaho Agency in what was then Indian Territory.

*Image: "The Snow-Fall" in The Cheyenne Transporter (Darlington, Indian Territory), 10 February 1883.*

waypoints.title: Milking Time
waypoints.body:
One could find advice, jokes, and poetic reflections about milking time reprinted in nineteenth-century newspapers. One example lists practical steps farmers could follow to increase their cows' yield.

*Image: Advice about milking in The Vancouver Independent (Vancouver, WA), 14 October 1876.*

waypoints.title: Your Forehead
waypoints.body:
Comparing his beloved's forehead, even favorably, to "the elbow of an old coat" is not likely to cause her to swoon. But the line invokes a common metonym in poetic texts. A more earnest poem, "Souls, Not Stations," was one of the most widely-reprinted in our findings; in it, lazy (and thus ungodly) people who are "fattened…by the sweat of others' foreheads" are promised retribution when God's "truth and justice" prevail.

*Image: "Souls, Not Stations" in The Kansas Herald of Freedom (Wakarusa, Kansas Territory), 17 February 1855.*

waypoints.title: A Chunk of Parian Marble
waypoints.body:
The reference to "Parian marble" recalls ancient Greece and Rome, subjects often discussed in reprinted historical texts. One cluster of reprints dismisses Rome's statues, monuments, games, and processions in favor of the civilization's less obvious achievements in "the lower sphere of material life."

*Image: "How the Romans Lived" in The Weekly Arizona Miner (Prescott, AZ), 25 December 1869.*

waypoints.title: Home-Made Sugar
waypoints.body:
We found eighty-nine reprints of a recipe for home-made whitewash, though only three of them call for sugar — a reminder of how reprinted texts, while essentially the same, were nevertheless altered in numerous ways as they circulated through the newspaper network.

*Image: "A Brilliant Stucco Whitewash" in The Sunbury American and Shamokin Journal (Sunbury, PA), 12 December 1840.*

waypoints.title: Tongue Wag
waypoints.body:
Though in our context the wagging of the lover's tongue is probably benign, newspapers made their living off wagging tongues while also deploring the practice. A frequently reprinted piece outlines the damage a wagging tongue could do — interestingly, it ran in several newspapers that often excoriated rival editors for their own personal, political, and moral failings.

*Image: "Pass It Along," from the Plymouth Weekly Democrat (Plymouth, IN), 22 December 1864.*

waypoints.title: Thrifty House Wife
waypoints.body:
Thrift was an important topic in the nineteenth-century paper, whether directed at the business or the domestic sphere. One typical advice-column example counsels readers to pursue slower but safer paths to financial security, to practice "thrift" rather than "speculation."

*Image: "Save" in The San Marcos Free Press (San Marcos, TX), 16 February 1882.*

waypoints.title: Sorgum Molasses
waypoints.body:
Newspapers also regularly printed short stories, such as Mark Twain's "Jim Wolf and the Tom Cat," reprinted in at least 40 newspapers, which involves its titular character, the titular animals, and some "hot candy molasses."

*Image: "Jim Wolf and the Tom Cat" in The Pacific Commercial Advertiser (Honolulu, Hawaii), 4 March 1871.*

waypoints.title: Churn Dasher
waypoints.body:
Our project is not primarily about advertisements, but on occasion ads are long enough to show up in our data. One of these is an ad for the Finley Churn-Dasher, which shows up in many small clusters, often accompanied by an illustration of the churn-dasher along with an explanation of its abilities at flopping up and down (like our young lover's heart).

*Image: "Churn Dasher," from the Public Ledger (Memphis, TN), 6 November 1867.*

waypoints.title: Young Goats
waypoints.body: A fascination with far-flung parts of the world, particularly Israel, characterizes many texts that circulated frequently in the nineteenth century. In our data, most mentions of young goats come from our love letter, but we also see a piece attributed to Wilde's Narrative about shepherds in Judea — one of the few pieces where we can say with some confidence that we know its first printing, in William Robert Wilde's book about his journeys around the Mediterranean. Though it is not a large cluster in our data, searching for it elsewhere (such as Google Books) shows that this piece also circulated widely in religious periodicals.

waypoints.title: Spanish Needles and Tow Linen
waypoints.body:
Trousers weren't the only thing made from tow linen — a commonly reprinted text in our data references tow linen in a recipe for making currant wine. Recipes were a very commonly reprinted type of text.

Spanish needles, also known as beggars' ticks, are plants with small thorny prickers, as we learn from a botanical piece reprinted a few times in the 1880s.

waypoints.title: Sea of Glory
waypoints.body:
The phrase "sea of glory" appears in several different types of reprinted texts in our data, including a parody of a speech by Cardinal Wolsey in Shakespeare's Henry VIII, adapted to the situation of an American electoral candidate waiting on the favor of his constituents.

A more commonly known use of the phrase appears in the hymn "From Greenland's Icy Mountains," written by Reginald Heber in 1819 and set to music by American hymnster Lowell Mason — considered one of the first missionary hymns ever written, but also appropriated by abolitionists, particularly its last stanza, where Heber's message of salvation for all people was reframed as freedom for all people as well. This excerpt appears in a letter to the editor published in the Anti-Slavery Bugle on January 5, 1856, among other issues of the same newspaper.

*Image: From the Rock Island Daily Argus (Rock Island, IL), 6 November 1890.*

*Image: From the Anti-Slavery Bugle (Salem, OH), 5 January 1856.*

waypoints.title: Hairs in a Blacking Brush
waypoints.body: Newspapers were full of advice on household problems, such as keeping one's shoes pliable and waterproof. Various solutions made the rounds of papers: one article recommended washing and oiling shoes monthly; another, a mix of tallow and rosin; still another warned against using only grease, lest it admit water more readily; one, dismissing the rest, suggested that simple castor oil would do the trick. Despite their competing claims, editors were evidently willing to let readers decide for themselves which technique gave the blackest, most waterproof footwear.

waypoints.title: Blue Bottle Fly
waypoints.body:
When a poem or anecdote gained popularity in the press, parodies usually weren't far behind. We can see this in the life of the very popular song "The Last Rose of Summer," printed and referenced in the newspaper press probably hundreds of times. The parody here deals with a subject much more prosaic — the blue-bottle fly — and though nowhere near as popular as the original, it nevertheless found an audience among readers of several newspapers.

*Image: "'Tis the Last Rose of Summer," in the New-York Tribune, 1 October 1911.*

*Image: "The Last Fly of Summer," from the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer, 4 December 1852.*

waypoints.title: A Glass Tumbler
waypoints.body:
Even something as seemingly innocuous as a "glass tumbler" can send a researcher in a variety of directions. In 1843 a new tariff was imposed on the import of glass tumblers from Germany, which led to an increase in domestic production, according to the New-York Tribune.

One piece, echoing the bumble bee whirling about under a glass tumbler here, suggests that a dozen fireflies from Jamaica "enclosed within an inverted glass tumbler" makes for an excellent reading lamp. And glass tumblers appear in an incredible (and satirical) inventory of items stolen from a New York shop by a woman "apparently about fifty years of age" — among the other items: "two ladies caps, one hat feather, one worsted hood, two pairs of worsted mitts, one dozen spools of cotton…" and, eventually, "a copy of Bishop Onderdonk's trial." That refers to the trial of Benjamin Treadwell Onderdonk, Bishop of the Episcopal Diocese of New York, accused of making improper advances toward several women — a story that turns up in a number of clusters in our data.

*Image: "Tariff—Glass Tumblers" in Burlington Free Press (Burlington, VT), 15 December 1843.*

*Image: "Fireflies of Jamaica" in The Cambria Freeman (Ebensburg, PA), 29 April 1869.*

*Image: "Walking Variety and Provision Store" in Sunbury American and Shamokin Journal (Sunbury, PA), 15 February 1845.*

waypoints.title: A Hot Whiskey Punch
waypoints.body:
Whiskey appears in reprinted texts of many kinds, from home remedies to jokes to scientific articles. One example is a joke — and a racist one — that is also an example of temperance literature. The temperance movement worked to persuade Americans away from alcohol, and in some cases to ban it through political action; Prohibition was the largest reform movement of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, finally culminating in its passage in 1919.

*Image: "Temperance Anecdote" in The Staunton Spectator (Staunton, VA), 16 October 1866.*

waypoints.title: The Presbyterian Steeple
waypoints.body:
In the early nineteenth century the vast majority of Americans belonged to Protestant Christian denominations, and readers would have expected to find religious pieces even in newspapers not explicitly devoted to a particular sect. Given the pervasiveness of Protestant thought in the country, denominational differences among American Protestants were much discussed — sometimes to sort right ideas from wrong, and sometimes, as in one widely-reprinted poem, to decry the importance of such distinctions altogether.

*Image: "No Sect in Heaven" in The Vermont Farmer (Newport, VT), 13 November 1874.*

waypoints.title: Blushing Like a Bride
waypoints.body:
Given newspapers' concern for domestic matters, "blushing brides" appear regularly in reprinted pieces. One example might be thought of as a short story, a fable, or even a travel narrative — all genres readers during the nineteenth century would have expected to find in their newspapers, even politically-oriented organs.

*Image: "A Fortunate Kiss" in The Plymouth Weekly Democrat (Plymouth, IN), 26 December 1861.*

waypoints.title: Beetles
waypoints.body:
Scientific oddities often made the rounds of the newspaper press, as in one short piece about "the muscular strength" of beetles — new knowledge about a familiar part of everyday life.

*Image: From the Burlington Free Press (Burlington, VT), 6 June 1856.*

waypoints.title: A Sorrel Horse
waypoints.body:
Given their centrality to nineteenth-century culture, it's no surprise that horses (and tips about them) appear frequently in reprinted newspaper texts. Like people buying cars today, people buying horses worried they weren't getting a good deal — that the horse dealer was cheating them. One widely-reprinted piece purported to give readers practical advice for telling just how old a horse was before buying.

*Image: "How to Tell the Age of a Horse" in The New North-west (Deer Lodge, MT), 16 December 1871.*

waypoints.title: Legions of Little Cupids
waypoints.body:
Unsurprisingly, Cupid appears in a great many clusters related to love and matrimony, including the widely-reprinted "fugitive poem" "The Young Widow," attributed to many different authors (or published anonymously) during the nineteenth century. One of the most likely claimants is Robert Josselyn, a lawyer, newspaperman, and soldier in the Mexican-American War and the Civil War, when he fought for the Confederacy.

*Image: "The Young Widow" in The Penny Press (Cincinnati, OH), 1 September 1859.*

waypoints.title: My Entire Anatomy
waypoints.body:
Biology and other scientific fields were frequent topics of reprinted newspaper pieces. Descriptions of various animals, including humans, were common, as in one widely-reprinted extract describing the muscles, bones, breathing, heartbeat, and other aspects of the human body.

*Image: "The Mechanism of Man" in The Morning Star and Catholic Messenger (New Orleans, LA), 8 May 1870.*

waypoints.title: Honey on a Bear's Paw
waypoints.body:
The joke below recounts a comical encounter between "two Yankees" and a bear, and features a figure well known to nineteenth-century readers: Jonathan, or Brother Jonathan, a symbolic representation of the United States and a precursor to Uncle Sam. Through the century Jonathan became a narrower figure — a mostly lighthearted stereotype of a Yankee, or New Englander. He even lent his name to America's first illustrated weekly newspaper, Brother Jonathan, launched in 1842.

*Image: "Time About" in The North-Carolina Standard (Raleigh, NC), 18 October 1848.*

waypoints.title: The Wind-Harp's Strains
waypoints.body:
The wind-harp (or Aeolian harp) was a common poetic image in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, perhaps most famously in a poem by Samuel Taylor Coleridge. The most widespread such poem in our findings is "The Closing Year," by George D. Prentice, best known as a Louisville, Kentucky newspaper editor. As Rufus Griswold's anthology The Poets and Poetry of America notes, Prentice also wrote poetry, much of it as a university student; pieces like "The Closing Year" were widely reprinted, likely due in part to their content and in part to Prentice's reputation among fellow editors.

*Image: "The Closing Year" in Rufus W. Griswold's The Poets and Poetry of America, 2nd Edition (1842).*

waypoints.title: Beds of Roses
waypoints.body: This record's original commentary was an easter egg rather than an annotation — an autoplaying YouTube embed followed by the line "Just kidding, y'all!" We'll leave that impulse noted here rather than reconstruct the embed.

waypoints.title: Burning Eloquence
waypoints.body:
Reprinted pieces of a more philosophical, religious, or reflective bent were often titled "An Eloquent Extract" in nineteenth-century newspapers — typically a somber but earnest reflection on life, mortality, and remembrance.

*Image: "An Eloquent Extract" in The Glasgow Weekly Times (Glasgow, MO), 6 September 1849.*

waypoints.title: Frogs and June Bugs
waypoints.body:
A reprinted prose poem warns "gals" to "beware of men in June…when frogs and Junebugs are in tune," lest they end up with their virtue compromised. It's a window onto common nineteenth-century attitudes about gender and sexuality: what begins as an idyllic scene becomes a threat of discipline through the press, ending with a warning to young women to be careful, "lest you get your names in the paper soon."

*Image: "A Tale of Love" in The Petroleum Centre Daily Record (Petroleum Center, PA), 7 October 1872.*

waypoints.title: Cold Lizards of Despair
waypoints.body:
The reprinted article "Giants of Olden Time" describes the discovery of "the skeleton of an enormous lizard" — what we would likely call a dinosaur — before becoming a "listicle" briefly describing a series of "giants" discovered throughout history. It was first published in Scientific American, which was deeply conversant with newspapers during its early decades, both as a source and a publisher of reprinted articles.

*Image: "Giants of Olden Time" in Scientific American, 17 April 1847.*

waypoints.title: Coffy's Patent Butter
waypoints.body:
Nineteenth-century newspapers included not only news but household tips, recipes, and other domestic items. Butter appears in one form or another in a huge number of reprinted texts we've identified. One typical example encourages parents to substitute apples for less healthful sweets — such as those listed in this very letter — at meal and snack times. Some themes, it seems, are timeless.

*Image: "Healthfulness of Apples" in The Daily Union and American (Nashville, TN), 24 December 1865.*

waypoints.title: Fresh Bacon in the Trap
waypoints.body:
As often happens to popular songs today, popular poems in the nineteenth century were frequently parodied — sometimes many times over, turned to different rhetorical purposes. William H. Lytle's "Anthony and Cleopatra" was one such poem, praised by editors as "one of the most masterly lyrics which have ever adorned American poetry." It was widely reprinted, and well-known enough to be parodied in pieces like "The Freedman's Complaint" — a racist parody, circulating largely in the southern states, that caricatures newly-freed Black Americans as lazy and criminal. "I am dying, Egypt, dying / Ebbs the crimson life tide fast" becomes, in this minstrel-show revision, "I am dying, Andy, dying / Corn and Bacon will not last!" It's a piece that demonstrates both how popular nineteenth-century texts were sustained through revision and reinterpretation, and the overt role many newspapers played in maintaining social and racial discrimination during the period.

*Image: "The Freedman's Complaint" in The Charleston Daily News (Charleston, SC), 16 April 1867.*

*Image: "Anthony and Cleopatra" in The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer (Wheeling, Virginia), 31 July 1858.*

waypoints.title: A Speckled Pullet
waypoints.body:
Perhaps claiming your beloved is fairer than a chicken — however speckled — is damning with faint praise, but this is not the only widely-reprinted piece to draw a metaphor between young women and pullets. A piece often titled "Idleness" circulated for five decades, demonstrating the impossible standards young women were often held to: rowdy and demure, pious and mirthful, stereotypically feminine and masculine all at once.

*Image: "Dow, on the Girls" in The Boon's Lick Times (Fayette, MO), 19 December 1846.*

waypoints.title: Cherry Tree
waypoints.body:
Given how many rural newspapers catered to agricultural readers, it's no surprise that many "viral texts" discussed crops of all kinds — though these pieces were also printed in more urban papers. Cherry trees appear in a number of clusters in our findings, in both practical and poetic contexts, including a few about George Washington's famous cherry-tree myth.

*Image: "Transplanting Trees" in The Los Angeles Herald, 15 April 1874.*

waypoints.title: A Poisoned Bedbug
waypoints.body: For many nineteenth-century Americans, bedbugs (among other pests) were an annoying fact of life, so it's no surprise that both stories about bedbugs and methods to poison them were frequently reprinted. One column in The Big Blue Union of Marysville, Kansas (11 November 1865) recommends the leaves of the elder plant for many things, and its juice to kill bedbugs and maggots in the home — the editors touting this as valuable enough to cut out and add to a scrapbook, "worth a year's subscription to any reader of this paper."

waypoints.title: The Last Resting Place
waypoints.body:
Given differences in both medical knowledge and funerary practices, most nineteenth-century readers encountered death more often than twenty-first-century people do. The most widely-reprinted texts we've found using the phrase "last resting place" are both poems: one a celebration of military valor, the other a more somber reflection on how people think about — and treat — their loved ones before and after death.

*Image: "If I Should Die To-night" in The Living Age (5 July 1873). The author, designated there only by her initials, was Arabella Eugenia Smith, who first published the poem in The Christian Union.*

waypoints.body:

To learn more about nineteenth-century newspaper reprinting, or our work in _Viral Texts_, see [our project publications](https://viraltexts.org/publications/) or our book, [_Going the Rounds_](https://manifold.umn.edu/projects/going-the-rounds)

waypoints.title: Marjorie's Almanac
waypoints.body: In at least one of its reprints, "Marjorie's Almanac" was attributed to T. B. Aldrich, and it sometimes ran under other titles, such as "Pleasanter Than All." You can find [reprints of this text in other newspapers here.](https://clusters.viraltexts.org/cluster/60136053764?search_term=majorie%27s+almanac)

waypoints.title: The Dashford Tragedy
waypoints.body:
We have only identified one other reprint of "The Dashford Tragedy" for the Viral Texts Project, in The _Ottawa Free Trader_ of 20 April, 1867. The _Free Trader_ claims to have reprinted the story, which it attributes to Clara Augusta, from The _Philadelphia Home Weekly_. Clara Augusta (or Clara Augusta Jones Trask) was a prolific nineteenth-century author whose other work does appear regularly in our database of reprinted texts.

*Image: "The Dashford Tragedy" by Clara Augusta in The Ottawa Free Trader (Ottawa, IL), 20 April 1867.*

waypoints.title: Hoofland's German Bitters
waypoints.body: In the Viral Texts Project we have worked to refine our algorithm to detect reprinted stories and poems, but ignore other kinds of text reuse like advertisements. Nevertheless, a few ads still manage to slip through, including a few other reprints of ads for Hoofland's German Bitters. So if you're suffering from Constipation, Flatulence, Inward Piles, Fulness of Blood to the Head, Acidity of the Stomach, Nausea, Heartburn, Disgust for Food, Sour Eructations, Sinking or Fluttering at the Pit of the Stomach, Swimming of the Head, Hurried or Difficult Breathing, Dimness of Vision, Dull Pain in the Head, Yellowness of the Skin and Eyes, Sudden flushes of Heat, or great depression of Spirits — then we have a cure for you!

waypoints.title: Crime in the Papers
waypoints.body:
Local crime stories often did not get much coverage outside their geographical region, and even in their own region usually boiled down to short snippets like this one, which we don't find reprinted in our data anywhere. Local news, even sensational local news like murder, doesn't seem to have had the necessary qualities to merit widespread reprinting. There were exceptions, though, as in the case of one George Hopkins, tried for the murder of his overseer's wife and slander against her — a story that circulated for more than 20 years, kept alive not by the murder itself but by the extraordinary lawyer, John Taylor, who materialized seemingly out of nowhere to defend the slandered woman. Most printings call it "The Volunteer Counsel," and the story is really about Taylor.

*Image: "The Volunteer Counsel," from the Plymouth Weekly Democrat (Plymouth, IN), 21 January 1869.*

waypoints.title: An Industrious Negro
waypoints.body: Only one other reprint of this news item appears in our database. Presumably this was considered newsworthy both for the amount of money earned — far more than would have been expected at the time — and because the farmer in question is African-American. As is clear elsewhere in this issue and the larger run of the paper, The _Raftsman's Journal_ clearly considered white readers its primary audience, and it propagated numerous stereotypes about both Black Americans and immigrant groups.

waypoints.title: Come to School
waypoints.body:
We have not found other instances of this joke reprinted in newspapers, but in general the press was very interested in the education of children — and, perhaps more to the point, the role of newspapers in that education. One of the single most widely-reprinted pieces we've found is a self-serving snippet claiming that Daniel Webster (or, in other versions, other famous Americans) had named newspapers as the most essential medium of a child's education. As newspapers sought subscribers, they were not shy about touting themselves as boons for developing minds.

*Image: "Daniel Webster on Newspapers" in The National Republican (Washington, DC), 24 April 1861.*

waypoints.title: A Good Rule
waypoints.body: "A Good Rule" was published under many titles, and in many expanded and abbreviated form. To see many other reprints of this text, [see our database of reprints.](https://clusters.viraltexts.org/cluster/2827738?search_term=%22i+owe+my+prosperity%22)

waypoints.title: Keep Warm and Save Your Life
waypoints.body: "Keep Warm and Save Your Life" was reprinted in various forms in more than 40 newspapers, which [you can view in our reprint database](https://clusters.viraltexts.org/cluster/667079?search_term=%22want+of+a+woolen+undershirt%22).

waypoints.title: Men Wanted
waypoints.body: We think of "listicles"—or articles in the form of lists—as products of the digital age and internet virality, but they were wildly popular in historical newspapers. "Men Wanted" was printed in many various forms in more than 200 newspapers between 1866 and 1874, [as you can see in our reprints database](https://clusters.viraltexts.org/cluster/1171211?search_term=%22want+of+this+age+is+men%22).

waypoints.title: Who Ate Roger Williams?
waypoints.body: This fanciful text describes both a historical and scientific curiosity. Browse reprints [in our database](https://clusters.viraltexts.org/cluster/5260761?search_term=%22who+ate+roger+williams%22).

waypoints.title: Manners
waypoints.body: Advice about manners were common to find in nineteenth-century newspapers. This one only appeared in [a handful of other newspapers](https://clusters.viraltexts.org/cluster/34361679287?search_term=%22carries+a+smile+on%22), but is a genre we find often in the project.

waypoints.title: Selling a Geologist
waypoints.body:
"Selling a Geologist" is an example of the genre [we call a "vignette" in our book, _Going the Rounds_](https://manifold.umn.edu/read/untitled-bd3eb0af-fdad-4dd6-9c94-3fd15d522ab6/section/06899e82-8f06-43d2-9fc9-ea04dffef886). 

---

*On "going the rounds":* we have not identified other reprints of this particular story in the Viral Texts Project (though it's likely some appeared in newspapers outside our corpus). But "going the rounds" was itself a common phrase in the period, used by editors to describe texts being frequently reprinted in their exchange papers — a nineteenth-century version of "going viral."

waypoints.title: Home Cheerfulness
waypoints.body: Domestic texts like "Home Cheerfulness" were staples of nineteenth-century newspaper, and particularly malleable as they circulated, with text being added or deleted to fit the page or the priorities of different editors. Nearly 200 such reprints of this texts can [be found in our database](https://clusters.viraltexts.org/cluster/4589183?search_term=%22as+flowers+need+sunbeams%22).

waypoints.title: Blessings of the Day
waypoints.body: This short affirmation was [reprinted in a number of other newspapers](https://clusters.viraltexts.org/cluster/8591523865?search_term=%22evils+bear+patiently%22) during the nineteenth-century, and made the rounds [again in the 1920s](https://clusters.viraltexts.org/cluster/4989841?search_term=%22evils+bear+patiently%22)

waypoints.title: Jokes
waypoints.body:
These are only a few of the jokes on this page—feel free to explore the page to find others. Jokes are often the hardest thing to translate between history and today, but they were widely reprinted then, just as they circulate in social media widely today. Because they are short, jokes can get jumbled up with other texts in our reprint data, but you can find reprints in our database of [the eight-hour a day man](https://clusters.viraltexts.org/cluster/8589964185?search_term=%22eight-hour+a+day+man%22) and the [printer's "chemise" joke](https://clusters.viraltexts.org/cluster/8590631193?search_term=%22wear+the+chemise%22) jokes. The pumpkin-turned-squash joke is likely too short to be captured by our reprint-detection methods, which we describe in [chapter 3 of _Going the Rounds_](https://manifold.umn.edu/read/untitled-883630b9-c054-44e1-91db-d053a7106ecb/section/ea1f849a-bac1-4e9d-85f4-149d0083a6a4).

The vegetable joke ("Toss up a pumpkin and it will come down a squash") only shows up in one other newspaper in our database, the Highland Weekly News from Hillsborough, Ohio — printed just under a month after this one, with the language changed ever so slightly from "Toss up a pumpkin" to "Throw up a pumpkin."

waypoints.title: Flirtation of the Heart
waypoints.body: This joke appeared with a few variations of punchline, as [you can see in these instances in our database](https://clusters.viraltexts.org/cluster/34363024553?search_term=%22flirtation+of+the+heart%22).

This punny joke appeared in several columns of jokes, often appearing alongside the same jokes in reprintings. [See instances in our database of reprints](https://clusters.viraltexts.org/cluster/6540495?search_term=%22a+tru-ant%22).

waypoints.title: Funny Scene in Court
waypoints.body: This humorous tale of a "scene in court" may be another example of the genre we call a "vignette." In [some reprints of the text](https://clusters.viraltexts.org/cluster/34366807150?search_term=%22cunning+ways+and+saucy+jokes%22), the prose uses details, such as the title of the New Orleans _Picayune_ newspaper, to imply the story is true.
